extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of crowd psychology, social scientists, political theorists, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length analysis of the immediate and preparatory factors that form the opinions of crowds (education, words/images/formulae, illusions, experience, reason) and guidance for how these factors can be used or changed to influence mass opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions must match national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Peoples are governed by their character, and institutions not intimately modelled on that character are merely a borrowed garment and transitory disguise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing institutions, assess whether they fit the inherited character of the people; identical institutions can produce prosperity in one country (e.g., United States) and anarchy in another (e.g., some Spanish-American republics). Attempts to impose institutions alone (through war or revolution) are ineffective unless they correspond to popular character; look instead to the underlying beliefs and sentiments of the crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction does not necessarily moralize or equalize
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to democratic dogma, instruction is not reliably capable of rendering a man more moral or happier, nor of changing his instincts or hereditary passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational systems by their measured social outcomes (crime rates, civic attitudes), not by the assumption that schooling alone will improve morality or create equality. Beware policies that equate increased schooling with moral progress; empirical statistics (e.g., higher criminality correlated with certain generalized instruction) should inform judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of rote, book-based ('Latin') education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education based on learning textbooks by heart and mechanical cramming develops obedience, stifles judgment and initiative, produces discontent with one's social station, and creates many diploma-bearing persons unsuited for practical life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an education system, look for overemphasis on memorization, examinations, and certificates; such systems tend to produce a restless, state-dependent class and a frivolous bourgeoisie. Prefer systems that foster judgment, initiative, and practical skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer professional/vocational/apprenticeship instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional instruction (apprenticeship, object lessons, workshop training) develops intelligence through direct sensory impressions and hands-on experience, enabling practical initiative and enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational programs should include early, staged apprenticeships and practical exposure (workshop, factory, law office, hospital) so that students develop perception, practical skill, and the capacity for spontaneous enterprise. Assess curricula for opportunities for real-world practice and incremental technical training rather than prolonged abstract book-learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment should test judgment and initiative, not rote recall
rubrics_metrics.description: Examinations that demand the recitation of large amounts of book-learning on a single day create ephemeral, overworked students; such tests fail to measure the faculties required for life—judgment, initiative, character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating assessment systems, favor continuous, competency-based, and practical assessments over single high-stakes rote examinations. Watch for systems that convert young people into 'living repertories' for exam day but fail to produce lasting capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align education with labor market and occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that produce more diploma-holders than available positions create an army of educated unemployed who become a source of discontent and potential revolutionary sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational planning for realistic links to employment opportunities (technical training, apprenticeship paths). Avoid overproducing credentials that the state or market cannot absorb—such mismatch fuels social unrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and formulae evoke images independent of literal meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Words possess power because of the images they evoke; their influence on crowds can be independent of their precise sense—terms like 'democracy,' 'socialism,' 'liberty' are often vague yet magically persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In persuasion or political communication, assess which words summon favourable or unfavourable images in the target crowd. Use terminology deliberately to call up intended images; recognise that logical refutation often fails against emotionally-laden formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meanings of words vary by time, race, and social class
rubrics_metrics.description: The images evoked by the same words change across ages, races, and social classes; identical vocabulary may signify very different ideas to different groups (e.g., 'democracy' in Latin vs Anglo-Saxon contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before using terms to influence or evaluate public opinion, investigate the specific connotations those words carry for particular audiences. Tailor language to class- and culture-specific meanings; failure to do so leads to miscommunication and ineffective persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political advantage of renaming/rebranding
rubrics_metrics.description: Statesmen can make odious or unpopular institutions acceptable to crowds by baptizing them with new, popular, or neutral words (Tocqueville's observation that the Consulate/Empire clothed old institutions in new names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political messaging or institutional reform, consider renaming as a pragmatic tool to alter popular reception. Examples: transforming 'taille' into 'land tax', or recasting unpopular practices with neutral labels to reduce negative images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds prefer illusions to naked truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds have always sought illusions and often prefer them to truths; illusions (religious, social, political) have been central engines of civilisation and mobilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When trying to explain or predict mass behaviour, recognise the social necessity and staying power of illusions. Attempts to destroy popular illusions are likely to be resisted and to make the destroyer a victim; provision of compelling ideals or myths is often more effective than purely rational appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusions are politically potent and recruit followers
rubrics_metrics.description: Social illusions (like socialism in the author's time) gain power because they promise happiness and are championed by those willing to make grand promises to the ignorant or credulous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate movements and messages for their capacity to supply hopeful illusions; understand that the promise of an ideal can mobilise crowds more effectively than dry factual argument. Counter-messaging that ignores the emotional needs crowds seek is unlikely to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience is the principal way to fix truths in crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated, large-scale experience is almost the only effective process by which crowds accept truths and relinquish dangerous illusions; single historical examples or arguments are usually insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking durable change in mass opinion or behaviour, plan for repeated practical experiences or experiments (policy trials, collective experiences) rather than relying on argument or isolated historical lessons. Be aware of the high cost and repetition required (examples: French Revolution, major wars, long-term economic outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason and logic have limited direct influence on crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic and reason have little efficacy in persuading crowds; crowds are influenced primarily by unconscious sentiments, images, and repeated experience rather than by rational debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In public communication and policy persuasion, do not overestimate rational argument's power; instead design messages that speak to sentiments and images, and create experience-based evidence that can be repeatedly observed by the crowd.
